12.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a patient with a bone lesion?"
- "Age, then pain: night, rest, mechanical or not, getting worse?"
- "Swelling: when, growing, painful? Then fever, weight loss, cancer history."
- "Past lesion or radiation, family history, and any fracture after trivial trauma."

### The four ways a tumour presents
| Presentation | Typical story |
|---|---|
| Incidental | X-ray after an ankle sprain; no complaint |
| Swelling | noticed after a fall or while bathing a child |
| Pathological fracture | trivial trauma, mild pain for months before |
| Persistent pain | pain that does not go away |

- **Memory:** four doors — **found, felt, fractured, hurting**

### Age first
- Each tumour has its age range (12.6)
- New painful bone lesion over 40 → think myeloma and metastasis first

### Pain — the core of the history
| Ask | Worrying answer |
|---|---|
| When? | at night; wakes the patient |
| With activity? | no relation to exertion; present at rest |
| Course? | increasing over a short period |
| Relief? | none with analgesics |

- High-grade: short history, 1–3 months; low-grade: over 3 months (Miller)
- Night pain eased by aspirin or NSAIDs (anti-inflammatory drugs) → osteoid osteoma (Miller)
- Pain in a lesion that was painless → alarm

#### Is the pain significant?
- Significant pain limits daily activity (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Proof → muscle wasting: deltoid (shoulder), quadriceps (knee)
- Good muscles → the pain is not significant

### Swelling
| Ask | Meaning |
|---|---|
| When did it appear? | with the pain, or before it |
| Is it growing? | progressive swelling → suspect malignancy |
| Painful? | painful soft-tissue swelling → think sarcoma |

- Painless slow soft-tissue swelling → usually benign
- Bony lumps near the metaphysis, often multiple → hereditary multiple exostoses

### Constitutional, past and family
| Ask | Why |
|---|---|
| Fever, appetite, weight loss | malignancy or infection |
| Cancer: patient or family | metastasis; ask twice |
| Previous lesion or radiation | secondary sarcoma (Paget disease, irradiation) |
| Family history | multiple exostoses, neurofibromatosis |

- Post-irradiation sarcoma needs a latent period of at least 5 years (Nagah)

### Fracture through the lesion
- Pain in the same place 4–5 months before → pathological (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Pain the same or worse after 2–3 weeks of treatment → investigate now

[[FIG: Fig 12.1 — Pathological fracture, femoral lesion · 12.01

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | night, rest, mechanical, getting worse, analgesics |
| Swelling | onset, growth, pain, size changes |
| General | fever, appetite, weight loss |
| Past and family | cancer, radiation, old lesion, exostoses |

- **Red flags:** night pain, rest pain, growing swelling, weight loss
- **Memory:** **Age, Pain, Swelling, Systemic, Family and past**
- General interview → ch 1

12.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this swelling"
- "General first: wasting, skin, lumps, nodes, thyroid, breast, abdomen."
- "Then the swelling: site, size, shape, surface, edge, consistency, temperature, tenderness, mobility."
- "Then joint above and below, distal neurovascular status, and function."

- **Whole lump / swelling exam (video):** [▶ University of Kelaniya · 2:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=--PeBE3Qq3c)

### The route on one page
| Step | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| General | weight loss, skin, lumps, nodes, thyroid, breast, abdomen |
| Look | site, size, shape, skin, scars, wasting |
| Feel | temperature, tenderness, surface, edge, consistency, mobility |
| Special | fluctuation, pulsation, bruit, transillumination |
| Move | joint above and below |
| Neuro, Vascular | distal pulses, nerves over the lump |
| Finish | function; "I would examine the chest and abdomen" |

- General examination takes 3–4 minutes and may give the diagnosis (Prof Abosena)

### General examination
| Look for | Points to |
|---|---|
| Weight loss, cachexia | malignancy |
| Café-au-lait spots | neurofibromatosis, McCune-Albright (fibrous dysplasia) |
| Café-au-lait + multiple non-ossifying fibromas | Jaffe-Campanacci syndrome (Nagah) |
| Many bony lumps near joints | hereditary multiple exostoses (HME) |

[[FIG: Fig 12.2 — Café-au-lait patches; many exostoses · 12.02

#### Search for a primary
| Region | Check |
|---|---|
| Neck | thyroid; cervical nodes |
| Chest | breast lump; axillary nodes |
| Abdomen | mass, loin mass (kidney) |
| Pelvis | prostatic symptoms → urologist |

- Five carcinomas spread to bone: prostate, thyroid, breast, lung, kidney (Miller)
- **Memory:** **"BLT with a Kosher Pickle"** — breast, lung, thyroid, kidney, prostate

[[FIG: Fig 12.3 — Neck nodes and thyroid · 12.02

### Local examination — the swelling
#### Look
| Look at | Say |
|---|---|
| Site | which bone, which end, joint nearby |
| Size and shape | in centimetres; rounded, lobulated |
| Skin | colour, scars, sinus, biopsy scar |
| Muscles | wasting above and below |

- Move the joint: does the swelling change?

#### Feel
| Feel | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Temperature | warm → inflammation or infection |
| Tenderness | bony tenderness → significant lesion |
| Surface and edge | smooth, well-defined; or irregular, ill-defined |
| Consistency | bony hard, firm, soft, cystic |
| Mobility | fixed to bone, or moves over it |

- Deep to fascia or over 5 cm → sarcoma until proven otherwise (Campbell)

[[FIG: Fig 12.4 — Osteochondroma above the knee · 12.02

#### Move, neuro, vascular
| Check | Look for |
|---|---|
| Joints above and below | range, block, tendons catching on the lump |
| Soft swelling over an exostosis | bursa, or growth? |
| Distal pulses | popliteal lump pressing the artery |
| Nerves | peroneal at the fibular neck; distal paraesthesia |

### Finish
- Regional lymph nodes; then other bones for more lesions
- "I would examine the chest, abdomen and breasts, and image the lesion"

PITFALL — "examining only the lump"
- The diagnosis is often outside the limb: breast, thyroid, kidney
- Say → "**I would complete a general examination looking for a primary.**"

12.03.t: 12.3 Reading the X-ray at the bedside
12.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "describe this X-ray"
- "Where is it? What is it doing to the bone? How is the bone reacting?"
- "Is there matrix? Is there a soft-tissue mass? Benign-looking or aggressive?"

- X-ray first, not MRI (magnetic resonance imaging); it may make the diagnosis
- CT = computed tomography; each tumour in detail → Bone Tumours book, ch 1

### The scheme in five questions
| Question | Answer with |
|---|---|
| 1. Where? | which bone and part; cortex, medulla or surface; central or eccentric |
| 2. What is it doing to bone? | lysis or sclerosis; margin well- or ill-defined |
| 3. How is the bone reacting? | sclerotic rim; periosteal reaction |
| 4. Matrix? | cartilage dots and rings; fluffy osteoid |
| 5. Soft tissue? | mass beyond the cortex |

- **Memory:** **Where, What, Reaction, Matrix, Mass** (Prof Abosena)

#### Site in the bone
| Site | Think of |
|---|---|
| Epiphysis | chondroblastoma, infection, giant cell tumour (GCT) |
| Diaphysis | fibrous dysplasia, Ewing sarcoma, metastasis, myeloma, lymphoma |
| Metaphysis | everything else — most tumours |

[[FIG: Fig 12.5 — Location chart · 12.03

#### Margin and zone of transition
| Margin | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Well-defined, sclerotic rim | slow; least aggressive |
| Well-defined, no rim | more active |
| Partly ill-defined | more aggressive |
| Moth-eaten or permeative | most aggressive |

- Traceable with a pen → well-defined (geographic)
- The faster the lesion, the less clear the margin

[[FIG: Fig 12.6 — Narrow versus wide zone of transition · 12.03

#### Periosteal reaction
| Reaction | Means |
|---|---|
| Continuous, solid | less aggressive |
| Thin lamellated | benign, stress fracture, healing |
| Interrupted | aggressive, most likely malignant |
| Sunburst | very aggressive |
| Codman triangle | aggressive lesion — not diagnostic of sarcoma |

- Periosteal reaction takes 10 days to 3 weeks to form (Prof Abosena)

[[FIG: Fig 12.7 — Periosteal reactions; Codman triangle · 12.03

#### Matrix
- Cartilage: dots, rings and arcs
- Bone: fluffy, cloud-like density

[[FIG: Fig 12.8 — Matrix patterns · 12.03

### Benign or aggressive?
| Feature | Benign | Aggressive or malignant |
|---|---|---|
| Margin | well-defined, sclerotic | ill-defined, moth-eaten |
| Cortex | intact | perforated |
| Periosteal reaction | solid | interrupted |
| Soft-tissue mass | absent | present |

[[FIG: Fig 12.9 — Benign versus malignant features · 12.03

#### Benign stages: latent, active, aggressive
| Stage | Behaviour | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Latent (1) | inactive, found by chance | non-ossifying fibroma |
| Active (2) | grows inside the bone | simple bone cyst, aneurysmal bone cyst |
| Aggressive (3) | breaks out of the bone | GCT |

- **Memory:** latent sleeps, active grows, aggressive breaks out
- Malignant stages: 1, 2, 3 by grade, compartment, metastasis

[[FIG: Fig 12.10 — Latent, active and aggressive lesions · 12.03

### When to order MRI
| Order MRI | No MRI |
|---|---|
| X-ray not diagnostic | spot diagnosis: non-ossifying fibroma, osteoma, fibrous dysplasia |
| Pain, bony tenderness, cortex involved (Kasr Al-Ainy) | no pain, intact cortex |

- Symptomatic, normal X-ray: 30–50% of bone must go first (Prof Abosena)
- MRI: with contrast, whole bone, joint to joint → skip lesions

[[FIG: Fig 12.11 — Worrying cartilage lesion signs · 12.03

### Staging investigations
| Step | Test |
|---|---|
| Local | X-ray, then MRI with contrast of the whole bone |
| Chest | CT chest |
| Skeleton | bone scan (solitary or multiple) |
| Last | biopsy |

- No tumour markers in sarcoma; alkaline phosphatase and LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) = prognosis only

#### Suspected metastasis — extra tests
| Suspected primary | Test |
|---|---|
| Prostate | prostate-specific antigen (PSA) |
| Female | CA-125 |
| Colorectal | carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) |
| Parathyroid | parathormone, serum calcium |
| Myeloma | Bence Jones protein, protein electrophoresis |

- Imaging: CT chest, abdomen and pelvis; mammography in women
- PET-CT in equivocal cases

[[FIG: Fig 12.12 — Skip lesion on MRI; metastases on bone scan · 12.03

PITFALL — "ordering a biopsy first"
- Biopsy before staging spoils the MRI and may contaminate the limb
- Say → "**I would stage first; biopsy is the last step.**"

12.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what does a tumour station test?"
- "Describe a swelling, examine the nodes, describe an X-ray, or score a lesion."
- "Every swelling: fluctuation, pulsation, transillumination before you leave it."

### Is this lump benign or worrying?
#### Swelling description
- **Aim:** a full, ordered description of any lump
- **How:** inspect site, size, shape, skin; palpate tenderness, consistency, edge, depth, mobility
- **Positive:** deep to fascia or over 5 cm → sarcoma until proven otherwise
- **Why:** each item separates benign from aggressive
- **Video:** [▶ University of Kelaniya · 2:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=--PeBE3Qq3c)

[[FIG: Fig 12.13 — Swelling scheme · 12.04

#### Lymph node examination
- **Aim:** nodal spread or a primary elsewhere
- **How:** roll fingers over the regional group, then the others
- **Positive:** enlarged, hard, fixed nodes → metastasis or infection
- **Why:** some sarcomas spread to nodes — rhabdomyosarcoma, epithelioid, synovial (Campbell)
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 5:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WSi42C9Nzv8)

| Limb | Groups |
|---|---|
| Upper | supracondylar (epitrochlear), axillary, cervical |
| Lower | popliteal, inguinal |

[[FIG: Fig 12.14 — Axillary and supracondylar nodes · 12.04

### Is it fluid, blood or solid?
#### Transillumination
- **Aim:** is the lump a fluid-filled cyst?
- **How:** darkened room; penlight against the side of the mass
- **Positive:** light passes through → cyst (ganglion)
- **Why:** clear fluid transmits light; solid tissue blocks it
- **Trap:** useless for tiny ganglia (Reider)
- **Video:** [▶ Dr Thomas McClellan · 0:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-tDykaWI2W4)

#### Pulsatility and bruit
- **Aim:** is the lump vascular — pseudoaneurysm or vascular tumour?
- **How:** two fingers on the lump; then listen with the stethoscope
- **Positive:** expansile pulsation, thrill or bruit → vascular lesion
- **Why:** osteochondroma edge can injure the popliteal artery (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Trap:** a pseudoaneurysm may thrombose and stop pulsating

[[FIG: Fig 12.15 — Popliteal pseudoaneurysm beside an osteochondroma · 12.04

### "Describe this X-ray"
#### X-ray description station
- **Aim:** systematic description, then a short differential
- **How:** name, side, view; then where, what, reaction, matrix, mass (12.3)
- **Positive:** interrupted reaction, wide zone, soft-tissue mass → aggressive
- **Why:** examiners mark the order, not the diagnosis
- **Video:** [▶ Conceptual Orthopedics (Dr V K Gautam) · 6:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b2f-Z2AzYjg)

[[FIG: Fig 12.16 — Osteosarcoma: sunburst and Codman triangle · 12.04

### Will it break?
#### Mirels score
- **Aim:** impending fracture in a metastatic long-bone lesion
- **How:** score four items, 1 to 3 each; total out of 12
- **Positive:** score above 8 → prophylactic fixation (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Why:** fix before it breaks; complete staging first
- **Trap:** consider fixation already from 8 (Campbell)
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho M8 · 1:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BPE5gpAyaBs)

| Item | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Site | upper limb | lower limb | peritrochanteric |
| Pain | mild | moderate | functional |
| Lesion | blastic | mixed | lytic |
| Size (cortex) | < 1/3 | 1/3–2/3 | > 2/3 |

- **Memory:** **SPLS** — site, pain, lesion, size; worst = 3 each

[[FIG: Fig 12.17 — Mirels table; a lesion that later broke · 12.04

### Other tests
| Test | Point |
|---|---|
| Fluctuation | fluid moves between your fingers → cystic |
| Tinel test | tap the lump → distal tingling → nerve tumour |
| Sign of emptying | empties on pressure, refills → vascular lesion |
| Limb girth | wasting proves significant pain |

PITFALL — "calling a pulsatile lump a tumour and biopsying it"
- A needle into a pseudoaneurysm bleeds; check pulsation and bruit first
- Say → "**It is pulsatile; I would request a CT angiogram before anything else.**"

- **Positive:** score above 8 → prophylactic fixation (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Why:** fix before it breaks; complete staging first
- **Trap:** consider fixation already from 8 (Campbell)
- **Video:** [▶ Ortho M8 · 1:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BPE5gpAyaBs)

| Item | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Site | upper limb | lower limb | peritrochanteric |
| Pain | mild | moderate | functional |
| Lesion | blastic | mixed | lytic |
| Size (cortex) | < 1/3 | 1/3–2/3 | > 2/3 |

- **Memory:** **SPLS** — site, pain, lesion, size; worst = 3 each

| Test | Point |

| Fluctuation | fluid moves between your fingers → cystic |
| Tinel test | tap the lump → distal tingling → nerve tumour |
| Sign of emptying | empties on pressure, refills → vascular lesion |

PITFALL — "calling a pulsatile lump a tumour and biopsying it"
- A needle into a pseudoaneurysm bleeds; check pulsation and bruit first
- Say → "**It is pulsatile; I would request a CT angiogram before anything else.**"

12.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "two-minute tumour case"
- "Spot: age, site, swelling, scar. Do: tenderness, joint, nodes, neurovascular."
- "Say: one diagnosis, one differential, and the next step."

### Incidental latent lesion (non-ossifying fibroma)
- **Spot:** 15-year-old, ankle sprain; X-ray shows a fibular cortical lesion
- **Do:** lesion painless, no mass; neurovascular normal
- **Do:** film: eccentric, cortical, sclerotic rim, no expansion
- **Say:** "Latent non-ossifying fibroma; reassure. Differential: aneurysmal bone cyst."

- Heals by skeletal maturity; no staging needed
- Fracture through it → treat as any fracture; no routine graft

[[FIG: Fig 12.18 — Fibrous cortical defect, distal tibia · 12.05

### Enchondroma
- **Spot:** adult, knee complaint; incidental central lesion with calcified dots
- **Do:** pain? bony tenderness? Scalloping or expansion on the film?
- **Say:** "Enchondroma, distal femur. Differential: low-grade chondrosarcoma."

| Worry signs (course slide) | Then |
|---|---|
| Size over 7 cm | MRI |
| Cortical expansion | MRI |
| Endosteal scalloping | MRI |
| New pain in an old lesion | MRI, then curettage |

- Commonest tumour of the hand

[[FIG: Fig 12.19 — Enchondroma, popcorn calcification · 12.05

### Osteochondroma (solitary or multiple)
- **Spot:** child or teen, hard painless lump near the knee or shoulder
- **Do:** tenderness, joint range, impingement, neurovascular
- **Do:** search the whole skeleton — scapula and spine too (Prof Abosena)
- **Say:** "Pedunculated osteochondroma, distal femur. Differential: periosteal chondroma."

- Cortex and medulla continuous with the bone; points away from the joint
- Sessile = broad base; pedunculated = stalk

| Excise when | Example |
|---|---|
| Mechanical | tendons catching on knee bending |
| Pressure | peroneal nerve, popliteal artery |
| Malignant change | pain, growth after maturity |

#### Malignant change and HME
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Clinical alarm | pain, rapid growth, growth after physeal closure (Nagah) |
| Cartilage cap on MRI | normal ≈0.5 cm (Prof Abosena); over 1 cm worrying (Nagah) |
| HME criteria | more than 6 lumps, forearm deformity, metaphyseal broadening |
| Risk | solitary < 1%; HME 5–10% (Prof Abosena) |

- HME is autosomal dominant → ch 1 short case

[[FIG: Fig 12.20 — Pedunculated and sessile osteochondromas · 12.05

### Fibrous dysplasia
- **Spot:** child or young adult, bowed thigh; maybe café-au-lait spots
- **Do:** tenderness, deformity, limb length; puberty and skin → McCune-Albright
- **Say:** "Fibrous dysplasia, proximal femur. Differential: Paget disease."

- Ground-glass, central, thin cortex; shepherd's crook femur
- Paget: older patient, enlarged bone, mosaic pattern
- Treat deformity or pain: intramedullary nail, no graft

[[FIG: Fig 12.21 — Shepherd's crook deformity · 12.05

### Giant cell tumour around the knee
- **Spot:** mature young adult; knee pain and swelling
- **Do:** tenderness at the bone end, joint range, deformity, fracture
- **Say:** "Giant cell tumour, distal femur. Differential: aneurysmal bone cyst."

- Eccentric lytic lesion at the bone end, close to the joint
- Pathological fracture in 10–30% (Prof Abosena)
- MRI → core biopsy → extended curettage; destroyed joint → resection

[[FIG: Fig 12.22 — Giant cell tumour, distal femur · 12.05

### Osteosarcoma in a teenager
- **Spot:** teenager, pain 4 months, waking at night, no analgesic relief
- **Do:** tender knee swelling, joint range, neurovascular status
- **Do:** regional nodes; chest examination
- **Say:** "Suspected osteosarcoma, distal femur. Differential: Ewing sarcoma or infection."

- Metaphysis of femur, tibia, humerus; sunburst and Codman triangle
- Chemotherapy → wide resection → chemotherapy; no radiotherapy (Kasr Al-Ainy)

[[FIG: Fig 12.23 — Distal femoral osteosarcoma; whole-bone MRI · 12.05

### Metastasis or pathological fracture in an older adult
- **Spot:** over 40, fracture after trivial trauma, pain for months before
- **Do:** breast, thyroid, abdomen, loin, nodes; other bones tender?
- **Say:** "Pathological fracture through a metastasis. Differential: myeloma."

| Older patient, destructive lesion | First test |
|---|---|
| Myeloma | Bence Jones protein |
| Lymphoma | biopsy decides |
| Metabolic | calcium, parathormone |
| Metastasis | find the primary |

- First question: pathological or traumatic? Stage before fixing

[[FIG: Fig 12.24 — Pelvic and femoral neck metastases · 12.05

### Osteoid osteoma
- **Spot:** child, groin pain worse at night, eased by aspirin
- **Do:** localized tenderness, quadriceps wasting
- **Say:** "Osteoid osteoma, proximal femur. Differential: osteoblastoma."

- Nidus under 1.5 cm; larger → osteoblastoma (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Radiofrequency ablation; no core biopsy needed

12.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "present your case"
- "Age, site, duration, pain pattern; swelling findings; general findings; X-ray description."
- "Benign-looking or aggressive; my differential; then staging and biopsy last."

### Present it like this (course osteosarcoma case)
| Part | Say |
|---|---|
| History | "A teenage boy, distal thigh pain 4 months, waking him at night." |
| Swelling | "Minimal swelling, distal femur; no analgesic relief." |
| General | "No lymph nodes; chest clear; no other lumps." |
| X-ray | "Distal femoral lesion with a fracture; malignant look." |
| Verdict | "Aggressive lesion, likely osteosarcoma; I would stage, then biopsy." |

### Differential by age and site
| Age | Think of |
|---|---|
| Child, teenager | non-ossifying fibroma, bone cyst, osteochondroma, osteoid osteoma, osteosarcoma, Ewing |
| Young adult, mature skeleton | GCT |
| Over 40 | metastasis, myeloma, lymphoma, chondrosarcoma, metabolic |

| Iliac destructive lesion (Nagah) | Think of |
|---|---|
| Skeletally immature | Ewing sarcoma |
| Mature, with calcification | chondrosarcoma |
| Mature, no calcification | metastasis |

- **Memory:** young → sarcoma; mature knee end → GCT; old → metastasis and myeloma

### Biopsy — "what next?"
| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Last step, after staging | biopsy changes the MRI picture |
| Done by the treating surgeon | biopsy errors are commoner elsewhere (Campbell) |
| In the line of the definitive incision | the tract is excised with the tumour |
| Longitudinal, through muscle (Miller) | the tract stays excisable |
| Away from neurovascular structures | a contaminated bundle may cost the limb |
| Core needle, CT-guided | bone needs cells and matrix; no cytology |

- **Memory:** **last, by the surgeon, in line, through muscle**
- Culture what you biopsy; biopsy what you culture (Miller)
